authors: Abbie VanSickle The New York Times

text:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration can resume rapidly deporting immigrants to countries other than their own, the Supreme Court agreed Tuesday.

The one-page emergency ruling was unsigned and gave no vote count, as is typical in such cases. Although the justices cleared the way, for now, for the swift removals to continue, they also announced that the court would fast-track the case and hear oral arguments about it in December, setting up a final ruling on the issue next year.

Their decision to hear oral argument on the legality of sending thousands of immigrants to what are referred to as third countries, including nations that have faced accusations of human rights abuses, sets up another major test of the limits of executive power at the Supreme Court.

On the line will be a hallmark of President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda, a policy of sending people to countries where they have no ties, including Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Costa Rica, Honduras and the Central African Republic.

The court's three liberal justices noted that they would have denied the government's request to resume the deportations.

The justices asked the lawyers for the administration and the immigrants who challenged the policy to focus their briefing for the December argument on whether the lower court judge who had paused the swift deportations had the authority to do so, and whether the policy violated the Constitution and international protections against torture.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, celebrated the court's ruling. In a statement, he called it a "victory."

"A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike," he said.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the National Immigration Litigation Alliance and part of the team representing the immigrants, called the emergency decision "a devastating result." The court, she said in a statement, "has allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture."

But she pointed out that the court had agreed to hear full argument in December, saying that Tuesday's decision "does not decide that the policy is lawful."

The deportations had been blocked recently after a federal court ruled the administration could not deport migrants to third countries unless they were given an opportunity to contest their removals, including to voice concerns that they might be persecuted or tortured abroad.

The justices' ruling means that the administration can, for now, continue its program and conduct rapid deportations including to countries such as Equatorial Guinea, where U.S. deportees were hooded, bound and beaten by police, according to reporting by The New York Times.

The justices had weighed in previously on the administration's efforts to send immigrants to third countries.

In May 2025, the Trump administration asked the justices to step in and clear the way for third-country deportations after a federal judge in Massachusetts temporarily blocked the administration from sending people to countries not their own -- in that case South Sudan -- without the chance to object.

In a one-paragraph ruling, the court's conservatives allowed the administration to continue the deportations over the noted dissents of the three liberals.

Since then, the Trump administration has continued to deport immigrants under the program, including to authoritarian countries with histories of human rights abuses. So far, the administration has sent more than 25,000 people to third countries as part of its mass deportation efforts, according to a social media post by Percival.

In his brief, Solicitor General D. John Sauer characterized the third-country deportation program as "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."

Sauer wrote that the appeals court ruling had "created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations," including canceled deportation flights and disrupted delicate diplomatic negotiations with other countries.

Lawyers for a group of immigrants challenging their removals said in a brief that the Trump administration had ignored "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there."

They argued that the Trump administration could avoid any delays in its deportation program simply by "providing the notice and opportunity to be heard that the law requires."

text:
Three people died on Monday, September 28, off the coast of France while attempting an illegal crossing of the Channel to the United Kingdom, French authorities said.

"A shipwreck involving a taxi boat occurred today off the coast of Wissant," a seaside village in northern France, the prefecture said, using a term referring to a dinghy that approaches the beach from the sea to pick up migrating people in shallow waters off the beach. The initial death toll stood at three, it said.

A rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident, an Agence France-Presse correspondent said. A coach, as well as fire service and police vehicles, were deployed at the scene, they said.

France has long been a launchpad for migrating people without visas hoping to cross the Channel to start a better life in Britain. They pay smugglers thousands of dollars to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world's busiest shipping routes.

Three bodies were found last week after chaotic "taxi boat" departures of this kind in northern France. At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an AFP tally based on official French and British sources.

authors: Maanvi Singh, Will Craft, Andrew Witherspoon, Julius Constantine Motal

text:
Those who lived through it describe the ICE raids as a “siege” or an “occupation”.

At the height of the raids last year, agents in armored military vehicles rolled through residential neighborhoods. Masked agents patrolled public parks and stationed themselves outside elementary schools; squadrons of ICE agents snatched pedestrians off the streets.

Then, officers killed two US citizens during an ICE “blitz” on Minneapolis. After a public backlash, the Trump administration said it would try a new approach.

“I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch,” Donald Trump said in February. He chose a new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, who promised to cut the flash and fanfare. “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day,” he said at his Senate confirmation hearing in March.

Six months on, that’s what his agency has delivered.

Now ICE is anywhere and everywhere, embedded in all corners of everyday life.

A Cuban man in Miami who stepped outside his house to take out the trash was detained moments after he had dropped the garbage bag into the bin. An Ecuadorian father was arrested in Danbury, Connecticut, just after seeing his six-year-old son onto the school bus. People have been arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home.

Y, a Venezuelan native, was stopped at the Phoenix Sky Harbor airport by immigration officers whom he said wouldn’t tell him why he was being arrested, or accept proof of a judicial order expressly prohibiting deportation to his home country. Four days later, he was on an airplane departing to Venezuela. Just before takeoff, he was deboarded – ICE officers admitted they may have made a mistake.

Though agents appear to be moving with more stealth than they were before, ICE arrests are still, often, violent. Glimpses of that violence are – despite Mullin’s initial intentions – still making national headlines.

Last week, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Austin, Texas. The Venezuelan asylum seeker, who had received a deportation order after missing a letter to appear in immigration court, was discharged from a local hospital with a bullet still lodged near his spine and then taken to ICE detention. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents.

Still, for every arrest that breaks through into public view, countless others happen quickly, before anyone can notice. “The detentions are happening in a flash – we’re talking, like, 90 seconds from the time ICE shows up to that person being driven away,” Willis said. “And often they are moving very quietly, with very soft feet.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the US government agency that oversees ICE, declined to comment on how its tactics had changed. “DHS will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations, strategy or tactics,” said Chandler Rebel, a spokesperson for the agency. But Rebel confirmed the agency’s focus on airports, noting DHS is “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.

Bolstered by $75bn in funding from Congress, the Department of Homeland Security – the US government agency that oversees ICE – has more than doubled its workforce this year to more than 22,000 officers and staff. It has also vastly expanded its capacity by working with local police, sheriffs, highway patrol and even fish and wildlife agents. As of 15 September, ICE has signed more than 2,500 287(g) agreements.

ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before.

An expanded dragnet fueled by police partnerships

“The administration is able to essentially hide a multiplied ICE force not only in unmarked cars, and not only behind masks, but also within local law enforcement through the 287(g) program,” said Willis. “I call it the invisibilizing of immigration enforcement.”

Operations that now originate with local police are taking place across the country.

At the El Corralón bar in Memphis on 29 August, an operation that began as a police raid targeting illegal gambling and drugs turned into one of the largest sweeps of undocumented immigrants in Tennessee – 120 people were detained. Immigration agents worked with state law enforcement to execute search warrants at the bar related to drugs and gambling, and targeting the bar’s owner. But then, at 1am that night, more than a dozen agents walked into the bar, shut off the music, instructed everyone to gather on the dance floor and asked them one by one if they had legal status, according to witnesses.

A spokesperson for the DHS said partnerships with law enforcement were key to the agency’s immigration enforcement. “We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement works together with us,” said Rebel.

Lawyers across the US said they worry that local law enforcement aren’t adequately aware of the nuances of immigration policy. “People are getting detained if they don’t have their green card on them. They’re getting stopped even if they have legal status,” said Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an immigration attorney based in Austin.

Last month, her client Brian José Morales García, 25, was deported to Mexico despite repeatedly telling officers that he was a US citizen, born in Denver.

Morales García was on his way to work as an air-conditioning installation tech, riding with his boss, when officers from the Gillespie county sheriff’s department and the Texas department of public safety (DPS) pulled them over. Both law enforcement agencies were working with ICE. Morales García told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him. Days later, he was deported to Mexico.

Eventually, the federal government reached an agreement with Morales García’s lawyers to let him back into the country, after Lincoln-Goldfinch submitted documents proving his citizenship.

“We’re seeing a lot of racial profiling,” she said. Local law enforcement appear to be especially active in Hispanic neighborhoods, she said, or in areas where Latino construction workers gather.

“They might have their sights set on a big job site, in some neighborhood under construction, and just slowly patrol that site and just take people in day after day until nobody’s going to work there anymore,” she said.

‘New pathways to deportation’

The Trump administration has also relentlessly reshaped immigration policies and bent the country’s vast bureaucracy to advance its mass-deportation agenda and boost arrest numbers.

“In order to sustain those numbers, they have to create more categories of people who can be subject to detention,” said Willis. “They do this by creating new pathways to deportation.”

In recent months, the supreme court cleared the way for the administration to end temporary humanitarian protections for 350,000 Haitians and Syrians in the US and made it easier to end protections for a total of about 1.3 million immigrants from a number of countries designated for temporary protected status (TPS). Currently, about 170,000 Salvadorians living in the US are anxiously waiting for the administration to announce whether it will renew or axe the same protections for them.

At the same time, the administration unrolled a new tactic of scheduling “mega-master” hearings – mass hearings in immigration courts, scheduled at the last minute so that many people do not know to, or are unable to, attend their mandatory court appointments. The no-shows are then ordered removed from the country in absentia, making them immediately subject to arrest and deportation.

After attorneys began reporting such hearings in May, judges issued 53,808 removal orders in absentia in June – a 55% increase. More than 13,000 of those removal orders followed mass hearings with a hundred or more people, according to researchers Joseph Gunther and Brandon Marrow, who created the site bklg.org to track and analyze procedural immigration data.

In the coming weeks, the Trump administration is also expected to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners. It has implemented a rule allowing officials to block people from becoming lawful permanent residents if they or certain relatives use public benefits such as Medicaid, food stamps or even student financial aid.

It is also increasingly pursuing “third-country” deportation agreements, so it can arrest and remove immigrants who were previously immune to removal because a judge had deemed that they would face torture or persecution if they were returned to their home countries. Now, more than 23,000 people over the last year have been expelled to countries where they have never been and where they have no ties. Some of these deportations are to countries with civil unrest, political instability, armed conflict and known human rights abuses.

There are constantly shifting rules about who can or cannot be detained or deported, and for how long. And there are constantly shifting norms on who will be detained or deported.

On one day, a client might go to an ICE check-in and leave without incident, Willis said. The next day, a different client with the same immigration status might be detained. “It makes it very hard to counsel people,” Willis said. “It’s very hard to prepare people for what they can expect.”

Pressured to self-deport

Not everyone who is arrested is immediately deportable – many people have pending immigration cases, or legal status. Indeed, there is a wide gulf between the number of people ICE is detaining each month, and the number of people who are deported.

Many of the people who are arrested languish in detention for months. Others – even those who may have a good chance of gaining asylum or another legal status – choose to accept voluntary deportation rather than wait months or years for their immigration case to process.

Federal circuit courts are currently split on whether immigrants who came to the US without lawful admission, including many asylum seekers, can be detained indefinitely without access to bond hearings. In some states, including Texas, the prospect of spending years inside a detention center can wear on immigrants.

“Almost every single detained parent that I talk to has been pressured into signing a voluntary deportation,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch. “Because they are told that if they sign, they get to go home and they can choose what happens to their kids.”

The Guardian is not using full names in some instances to protect sources’ privacy and safety

In August 2004, the permit was exchanged for a permanent residence permit with an "indefinite" validity period.

According to the Supreme Court, under such circumstances, the migration authority effectively canceled the immigration permit by declaring the indefinite residence permit invalid.
text:
On September 16, 2026, the Supreme Court, composed of judges of the Cassation Administrative Court panel, considered case No. 640/9008/22 on the claim of a stateless person against the Central Interregional Department of the State Migration Service (SMS) in Kyiv city and Kyiv region and the State Migration Service of Ukraine. The ruling was adopted on September 16, 2026.

The dispute concerned the legality of the migration authority’s review of the grounds for issuing a permanent residence permit, which was originally issued in 2002 and exchanged in 2004 for an indefinite residence permit, as well as the decision to declare these documents invalid.

The issue is significant for law enforcement, as the case involved not only compliance with legislation during the initial issuance of the document but also whether the migration authority can, after many years, eliminate the consequences of violations it discovered without establishing specific unlawful actions by the person and without following the prescribed procedure.

Case circumstances

The claimant arrived from Iraq to Ukraine as the wife of a serviceman of the peacekeeping contingent of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. In 2002, she and her husband were documented with a stateless person’s travel document and a temporary permanent residence permit. In August 2004, the permit was exchanged for a permanent residence permit with an "indefinite" validity period.

After her husband’s death on February 17, 2021, the claimant applied for a permanent residence permit with a contactless electronic carrier. The application was sent to the State Migration Service of Ukraine. However, the migration authority conducted a document check and found that the personal file lacked documents confirming the grounds for obtaining an immigration permit.

On September 3, 2021, a conclusion was approved stating that the decision to document the claimant with permanent residence permits was made in violation of legal requirements. In particular, the case materials did not contain documents confirming the grounds for obtaining an immigration permit.

The migration authority also referred to discrepancies in personal data and the results of a photo image study, according to which the claimant and an Iraqi citizen who received the status of a person requiring additional protection in Ukraine are the same person.

Based on this conclusion, by order No. 141 dated September 7, 2021, the State Migration Service of Ukraine declared invalid and subject to seizure and destruction the permit dated October 9, 2002, and the indefinite permit dated August 20, 2004.

The claimant appealed the conclusion and the order, indicating, among other things, that the permit was issued by a state authority, exchanged in 2004, and remained valid for a long time, and that procedural shortcomings during its initial issuance cannot be attributed to her. She also argued that she did not commit unlawful acts that could be grounds for canceling the immigration permit.

The courts of first and appellate instances denied the claim. They reasoned that the decision to document the claimant was made in violation of legal requirements, and therefore the permits were lawfully declared invalid according to paragraph 73 of Procedure No. 321.

Position of the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court first focused on the legal nature of the permanent residence permit and the permitting procedure.

The Court noted that according to the rules in effect at the time the claimant received the indefinite permit, documents submitted included, among others, a copy of the decision granting the immigration permit and other specified documents.

The Court stated that this indicates: without submitting the documents specified by this norm, in particular without an immigration permit, obtaining a permanent residence permit in Ukraine is impossible.

At the same time, the Court distinguished between canceling a permit and declaring it invalid.

The Supreme Court indicated that the migration authority may both cancel a permit and declare it invalid, with cancellation occurring together with the cancellation of the immigration permit to Ukraine pursuant to Article 12 of Law No. 2491-III, while in the case of declaring the permit invalid, Procedure No. 321 obliges the authority to establish the presence or absence of grounds for the person’s further temporary lawful stay in Ukraine.

The Court separately emphasized the obligation of the state authority to prove the legality of its decision.

The Court noted that in administrative cases concerning the illegality of decisions, actions, or inaction of a public authority, the burden of proof regarding the legality of its decision lies with the defendant.

The Supreme Court pointed out that in this case, primarily the migration authority bears the burden of proving the legality of its actions and decision, since since 2002 the authority did not detect the absence of the claimant’s immigration permit, and in 2021 such a permit disappeared, considering that during this time the claimant repeatedly applied to the migration authority and received other documents.

According to the Supreme Court, under such circumstances, the migration authority effectively canceled the immigration permit by declaring the indefinite residence permit invalid.

The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts did not establish what specific unlawful actions of the claimant caused the cancellation of the immigration permit by default and the issuance to her in 2004 by the migration authority of an indefinite permanent residence permit in Ukraine in violation of legal requirements.

At the same time, the Court referred to its previously established approach to Article 12 of Law No. 2491-III.

The Court noted that this provision sets out the list of grounds for canceling an immigration permit, from which it follows that the grounds for canceling an immigration permit can only be the culpable actions of the immigrant. Therefore, cancellation of the immigration permit is possible only if specific data are established regarding the commission or possibility of commission by the immigrant of unlawful acts under Article 12 of Law No. 2491-III.

The Supreme Court also drew attention to procedural guarantees during the decision-making on the cancellation of an immigration permit.

The Court indicated that the SMS, its territorial bodies, and subdivisions thoroughly study submissions regarding the cancellation of an immigration permit, request additional information if necessary, and may invite immigrants concerned to provide explanations.

Returning to the case circumstances, the Court noted that the immigration permit was canceled by the authority by default, and the permanent residence permit was declared invalid.

The Supreme Court stated that the defendant still has the obligation to establish the presence or absence of grounds for the person’s further temporary lawful stay in Ukraine, to conduct a comprehensive investigation of the circumstances under which the person stayed in Ukraine for 19 years based on a document issued by the same defendant. According to the Supreme Court, establishing these circumstances is impossible without obtaining explanations from the immigrant.

The Supreme Court noted that the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court has already stated: the need to correct a past "mistake" should not disproportionately interfere with the new right acquired by a person who relied on the legitimacy of the good faith actions of a state authority. State authorities that do not implement or comply with their own procedures should not be able to benefit from their unlawful actions or avoid fulfilling their duties.

According to the Court, the courts of first and appellate instances did not assess whether the defendant used its powers to make a decision that would meet the criteria of part two of Article 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure of Ukraine, nor did they verify whether measures were taken to implement paragraph 23 of Procedure No. 1983 and paragraph 73 of Procedure No. 321.

The Supreme Court pointed out that failing to invite the immigrant concerned to provide explanations regarding the cancellation of the immigration permit deprives the latter of procedural guarantees of direct participation in the procedure of making the relevant decision by the competent authority.

The Court also noted that the lower courts did not investigate a number of circumstances important for the correct resolution of the dispute. In particular, they did not assess the claimant’s arguments regarding the 2016 court decision that established the circumstances of issuing permanent residence permits to her husband, nor did they clarify the legal nature of the conclusion dated September 3, 2021, and whether it is an independent decision of the authority that directly produces legal consequences for the claimant.

Altogether, according to the Court, this indicated non-compliance by the courts with the principle of official clarification of all circumstances of the case, which made it impossible to establish factual circumstances important for the correct resolution of the dispute.

Therefore, the Supreme Court partially satisfied the cassation appeal, canceled the decision of the district administrative court and the ruling of the appellate administrative court, and sent the case for a new trial to the court of first instance.

Thus, the Court emphasized that a person’s long-term stay in Ukraine based on documents issued by the state does not in itself exclude the possibility of verifying the legality of their issuance, but such verification must be conducted following the established procedure.

If declaring a permit invalid effectively leads to the cancellation of the immigration permit, the grounds provided by Article 12 of the Law "On Immigration" and specific data regarding the relevant unlawful actions of the immigrant must be established. The migration authority must also conduct the necessary verification and ensure the person has the procedural opportunity to provide explanations.

text:
Republicans in some of the country’s most competitive midterm races are breaking with President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration agenda, publicly raising concerns about how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is carrying out operations in their states and districts.

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall called for ICE to coordinate with local law enforcement during operations in southwest Kansas, arguing that local agencies know their communities and can help keep people safe.

Local officials in Dodge City, Garden City, and Liberal said they were not notified beforehand about increased ICE activity. They said they learned of operations only after agents appeared in their communities.

Sen. Jerry Moran also urged federal-local coordination. Moran said DHS Secretary Mullin told him the warrants were intended to target people charged with criminal activity.

The pushback is also surfacing in other battleground areas. Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar said the administration’s immigration policies had “gone too far” in a campaign ad. In Texas, Rep. Monica De La Cruz highlighted her efforts to help a DACA recipient secure release from ICE custody.

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, now a Republican congressional candidate, also criticized ICE after saying the agency was wrongly seeking to deport a member of his family.

The reactions come as immigration enforcement becomes a potential political vulnerability for Republicans in battleground races ahead of the midterms, even as the issue remains closely tied to Trump’s agenda.

Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla said Republicans should back legislation requiring ICE agents to identify themselves, use body cameras and obtain judicial warrants for detentions if their concerns are genuine.

text:
DHS has dismissed a report that ICE officers were instructed to stop arresting illegal migrants who have no criminal convictions.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has dismissed a report that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers were instructed to stop arresting illegal migrants who have no criminal convictions or pending charges, saying “no one is off the table. ” The denial came after The Daily Wire reported on September 26 that ICE officers across the US had been told to stop arresting “non-criminals” for the time being. Citing agency sources, the report said ICE officers would instead focus on undocumented migrants with criminal convictions or pending criminal charges. According to The Daily Wire, the reported guidance would also end so-called “collateral arrests”, in which ICE officers can detain other undocumented migrants encountered while pursuing a specific criminal target. Under the reported change, officers would arrest only the identified target.

DHS rejects report of ICE arrest restrictions

DHS disputed the report on Saturday, sharing The Daily Wire report on X and calling the claim false. “This is false. No one is off the table,” DHS said. The department added that ICE would continue to arrest people who are unlawfully present in the US. “Anyone in our country illegally will be arrested and deported,” DHS said, while describing its current operations as a nationwide public-safety surge in sanctuary cities. The department said ICE officers were targeting undocumented migrants accused or convicted of serious crimes, including murder, rape, child sexual offences and gang-related crimes. The conflicting accounts leave it unclear whether any temporary internal guidance was issued to ICE officers or whether enforcement practices changed at specific locations.

What The Daily Wire reported

The Daily Wire said its sources described an apparent change in instructions to ICE officers that would limit arrests to undocumented migrants with criminal convictions or pending charges. The report quoted one ICE officer as saying the change was aimed at “calming things down” ahead of the US midterm elections. Another officer reportedly expressed opposition to the alleged instruction. The claims about the elections were based on anonymous sources and were not confirmed by DHS. Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin separately said he had spoken to nine ICE and DHS insiders who described “verbal guidance” being sent to ICE offices to avoid arrests of non-criminal migrants. Melugin said the guidance was later described as erroneous, with the situation attributed to a miscommunication over a policy of prioritising serious criminal offenders. The reported development comes amid a broader intensification of immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump. DHS has continued to announce arrests of illegal migrants with criminal convictions, while ICE recorded more than 50,000 arrests in August, according to data previously shared by DHS with The Daily Wire. For now, DHS clarifies that ICE has not been instructed to take non-criminal undocumented migrants off the table and says immigration arrests will continue nationwide.

End of Article

text:
When the South American man lay down in his bunk at night, he dreamed up ways to kill himself.

During his time locked up at the Aurora immigration detention facility, he said he witnessed violence and abuse, grew weak from hunger and was, eventually, brutally beaten by guards while handcuffed and suffering a panic attack.

The man, who spoke to The Denver Post on the condition of anonymity because he fears retaliation by the U.S. government, shared photos taken by his attorney from the encounter, after he’d been released from detention. The photos captured his swollen head, wrists, neck and arms covered in deep purple bruises.

Since his release, the man has endured nightmares, crippling anxiety and so much fear that he barely leaves his home. As he recounted his months in detention, he was reduced to shoulder-heaving sobs.

“I might be a big, tall man, but I am embarrassed to tell you that I am fragile now,” he said through tears and a Spanish interpreter. His attorney was also present. “They treat you as if you have no value. They treat you like trash, like you’re not a person. If I knew that being an immigrant in a first-world country that this was going to happen, I would have never came. Have mercy because there is no mercy here.”

Set between train tracks, highways and nondescript warehouses, Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s privately run Aurora facility has long been criticized for its conditions. Three detainees died there between 2012 and 2022. Geo Group, its operator, has been the subject of lawsuits, regular oversight visits from members of Congress, and reports and protests by advocacy groups and the American Civil Liberties Union.

Since President Donald Trump returned to office, the facility has ballooned to its highest possible capacity of 1,532 beds and has filled as many as 94% of them at a time, largely with people who have no criminal records. Reports about its poor conditions have increased, too: In interviews with The Post, current and former detainees described frequent fights and feelings of hopelessness. They say they’re often served inedible or rotten food that frequently gives them diarrhea. They speak of enduring summers without air conditioning and taking boiling-hot showers behind tattered and dirty curtains. Living quarters resound with sneezes and coughs, they say, either from the dust spewed from unreliable air conditioning or from the illnesses spread among the more than 12,000 detainees who have been booked into the facility since January 2025.

As the center’s population has increased, so have emergency calls and detainee trips to a nearby hospital, The Post found. Simultaneously, the oversight bodies charged with responding to complaints within the facility and others like it nationwide have largely been dismantled under the Trump administration, attorneys said.

The government has ended free legal training for detainees in the facility, sought to block congressional visits and enacted policies that have made it harder for attorneys to keep track of and speak with their clients. This year alone, two local health investigations, including one for tuberculosis, have been frustrated by the facility’s closed doors, and Geo amended its contract this month as it fought local oversight.

For many, the facility is a brief stopping point, a revolving door before they’re moved to another facility or readied for a flight out of the country.

Attorneys and advocates argued that the detention center’s conditions are intended to encourage people to stop fighting and accept that flight. Record numbers of detainees in the facility have done so, federal data shows.

“Their calculation is they need to survive,” immigration attorney Claire Noone said. “They have to get out to support their family. I am for the first time seeing more and more people look at their potential reality and look at the conditions of care they’re receiving and decide to take voluntary departure.”

But for others, it is a months-long limbo, where they fight their cases and ICE searches for ways to remove them.

To report this story, The Post spoke with eight current and former detainees and more than a dozen advocates, attorneys and experts. Five of them spoke on condition of anonymity or that only their first names be used out of fear of retaliation from the federal government. Some of the detainees had prior, low-level criminal records for driving under the influence or prior immigration violations. Two were arrested from county jails. The Post also confirmed details of their arrests and any prior criminal history using publicly released ICE data.

The Post reviewed 911 records, emergency reports and audio recordings from nearly two dozen ambulance and police calls to the detention center. The Post also used data from the Deportation Data Project in California, the Transactional Records Clearinghouse at Syracuse University and from ICE’s public reporting.

Nearly every detainee with whom The Post spoke had spent more than six months in the facility. Some had been there for more than a year. Two transgender women were told this month that they could either go to solitary confinement or accept regular housing with men, said AnnaRose Craig, an advocate with the American Friends Service Committee.

Several detainees said they didn’t understand what they’d done to deserve being kept there.

“If I stole something, if I – I don’t know – beat someone, killed someone, if I did something, and then based on that action, I’m in prison – I know why I’m here,” said Hossein Batooie, an Iranian who has lived legally in the U.S. since prior immigration proceedings more than two decades ago; he was released in April after 10 months. “What bothered me the most was, I never knew why they got me. Why? Why had I been arrested?”

Detainees describe spending their days playing cards, watching TV and trying to avoid fights or the ire of guards, whose behavior ranges from detached to aggressive. They wait for medical appointments and use tablets to talk with family members. A text message costs 35 cents. A day’s labor in a voluntary work program pays $1.

They mount protests for better food and medical care. Their mail is searched and scanned. They buy chips from the commissary to add texture to flavorless beans and twist Ramen packages into miniature shoes they hang from keychains or send to their families. They work on their legal cases and wait for the court hearings that will decide their future.

“They treat you as if we’re animals, basically,” said Daniel, a 32-year-old Venezuelan who’s been in the facility for more than a year and who spoke through an interpreter. “They basically treat you as if you’re an immigrant, you’re an illegal. They treat you with racism. They look at you as, ‘You’re an immigrant, I can treat you however I want.’ ”

Geo Group did not respond to an interview request. The company expects to earn roughly $3 billion in revenues this year, buoyed by the Trump administration’s efforts to arrest and deport millions of immigrants without legal status. It has operated the Aurora facility for nearly 40 years. It was the company’s first-ever detention contract.

In a July statement to the New York Times about conditions at a New Jersey facility, Geo spokesman Christopher Ferreira said that “in the event issues are identified, deficiencies are promptly addressed through established corrective action processes” required by ICE.

Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, declined an interview request. In response to a written summary of The Post’s findings, an unnamed representative for the agency broadly denied descriptions of unsafe conditions.

“All ICE detention facilities operate in strict accordance with all applicable federal detention standards for safety, sanitation and humane treatment in accordance with national detention standards,” the agency wrote. “ICE is committed to transparency and accountability and regularly conducts inspections to ensure the well-being of individuals in its care. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.”

Life in detention

In August, Daniel thought about his own death.

For two consecutive nights early in the month, a noxious, gas-like odor filled the cell he shared with other detainees. The smell was so strong, and he was so convinced it was a gas leak, that he thought if a match were lit, the whole room would explode.

They’d banged on their cell door, but guards told them it was nothing. The fire department came and said there was no gas leak. But Daniel remembered hearing about the six people who’d died at a dairy farm after being exposed to gas last year.

He barely slept, and later called his wife and warned her that something might happen to him. They’d come to the U.S. together from Colombia, where they’d run a restaurant after moving there.

“I’m afraid,” Daniel remembered telling her. “And I want you to know, in case I do die, this is why I died.”

Daniel and two other men who also smelled the odor this summer haven’t detected it since. Like tuberculosis quarantines, medical treatment and nearly everything else in the facility, the odor became the latest in a series of incidents over which detainees had no control and little information.

“The conditions inside the facility are not good right now,” said Monique Sherman, detention program managing attorney at the Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network. “We are seeing people who are sick, people not able to access medical care, and people who are being assaulted, and most of our clients don’t feel comfortable talking to us about something if somebody who works at the facility is listening.”

Showers blast water so hot that two people told The Post it felt like it would burn the hair off of their head. Bathrooms were dirty and appeared moldy. Shower curtains were so torn that one man said detainees would rip their own sheets to repair them for an inkling of privacy.

The air conditioning didn’t work for weeks over the summer, several people said, just as it hadn’t the summer before. One man, a young Guatemalan, said he would regularly sleep on the floor in his underwear because the ground was cooler.

It felt like “boiling in a pot,” he said.

He worked in the kitchen for access to better food. Food is a constant issue: Beans are the most consistent staple of detainees’ diets, watery and flavorless. Fresh fruits and vegetables are vanishingly rare; lettuce, frequently past due, is more common.

Food was often undercooked, the Guatemalan said. Stomach issues and diarrhea are common, even for people who’ve been in the facility for months. Batooie, 61, said they once received sliced apples, but they were moldy.

In its statement, the Homeland Security Department said meals are provided by dietitians. The agency said the facility has functioning air conditioning and never reached dangerous temperatures, and that fans and ice water were given to people detained there. It said ICE is regularly audited and that detainees are given proper meals, quality water, medical treatment and opportunities to communicate with families and attorneys.

Sometimes, there would be arguments and fights over the food, said Gabriel, a Mexican man arrested at a Denver-area Home Depot who was released this year. He’s been in the U.S. for more than 30 years, he said.

One detainee was stabbed in May, and the Aurora Police Department has taken “numerous” reports about fights at the facility in the past 18 months, a spokesman said. 911 calls reviewed by The Post described two sexual assault reports this year, one on behalf of a transgender detainee. Four April calls reported apparent overdoses, three of them believed to be intentional.

The Guatemalan kitchen worker, who is gay, said he was threatened with physical or sexual assault by other detainees and that he was bullied, including by staff. Gabriel and Batooie both said new arrivals would be greeted with jeers of “Vaseline” from other detainees, which Batooie took as a threat of sexual assault.

Fights broke out over the TV and the tablets that serve as detainees’ primary lifeline to their families and to the outside world.

“Everyone wants to speak with their family, everyone wants to speak with their kids, so that causes situations amongst the detainees,” said Ronald Aguirre, who has been in the Aurora detention center for more than a year.

He and others said guards didn’t try to defuse tensions before fights broke out; some speculated that guards wanted the tension. Detainees then “handle (arguments) among ourselves,” Aguirre said through an interpreter.

To break up those fights or protests mounted by detainees, Geo guards used pepper spray or brandished a gun that fired rubber or plastic bullets, Daniel and others said. They sprayed detainees full in the face, said Rony Chavez Martinez, who’s been in the U.S. since he was 10. He was arrested in Maryland last summer after getting into a fight with a coworker. He was transferred to ICE custody and has been detained in Aurora for more than a year.

Gabriel remembered watching from a window as men in another pod, who’d protested the food, were carried bloodied and handcuffed to solitary confinement after an altercation with a female guard. Aguirre said he’d seen guards use pepper spray “plenty of times.”

Rooms are searched and detainees’ few belongings are scattered or trashed, they said. Sleep was difficult in an “environment that never shuts off,” Batooie said. Group punishments are common. So, too, is the use of solitary confinement.

Batooie said he was called an anti-Arab slur by a guard and saw a guard verbally abuse a Muslim detainee, blaming him for conflict in the Middle East. The South American man who left detention with bruises recalled guards comparing stats on how many immigrants they had caught and how long it took to bring them down.

“We understand that we’re detained,” Daniel said. “If you demand respect, give respect. They ask for it, but they don’t give it. And we understand that — they don’t respect you.”

Medical delays

Protests were common — several men called them “strikes,” which mostly came in the form of refusing to participate in Geo’s regular head counts. Sometimes they’d refuse to eat or send the food back. In May, after one detainee was stabbed and the facility was put on lockdown, 51 detainees signed a letter criticizing the conditions and likening them to torture.

Daniel said they had protested last year to get more electronic tablets so they could talk to their families and curb the fights. Sometimes, guards took away people they perceived to be leaders.

Often, detainees banged on their doors and walls to get the guards’ attention for others who were sick and hadn’t received help. Several men complained about the lack of medical attention, a common issue raised by attorneys and advocates for years.

Gabriel said he had lost all of his molars because of the dental care, and that he had a friend who developed fungus on his feet. The man didn’t receive treatment until “the meat was falling off of his foot.”

In its statement, the Homeland Security Department said detainees were not denied medical care.

The facility has a history of disease outbreaks, including mumps and chickenpox. The Adams County Health Department confirmed a case of tuberculosis in the detention facility in June; the agency’s attempt to investigate the infection has since escalated into an ongoing fight between public health officials and the facility over outside inspectors’ ability to access the detention center and its occupants.

Detainees said a housing unit was placed on quarantine this month after they were told they were exposed to the disease. Immigration attorney and University of Colorado law professor Violeta Chapin said one of her clients was vaccinated against tuberculosis without his permission.

Lucie Donovan fought for her husband’s release from the Aurora ICE facility for more than a year, an effort chronicled in a Post story this year. But tuberculosis made them give up the fight, she said.

Her husband, Juan, was arrested by ICE on Feb. 5, 2025, during Denver’s most high-profile immigration raid since Trump returned to office. He had overstayed a work visa and had no criminal history. His immigration attorney, Anya Lear, said that was a common issue that would not have warranted detention under a different federal administration.

Juan endured rotten food and deteriorating health and inadequate medical care within the Aurora facility, he said in an interview with his wife. He said he was sent to solitary confinement after a detainee stabbed him.

Once Juan told Donovan someone in his housing unit had tuberculosis, she said that was their final straw.

“This is not the Oregon Trail. Why are we dealing with tuberculosis? What the hell?” Donovan said. “It started to feel like life or death.”

Juan put in for voluntary departure and was transferred to a detention center in Louisiana before being released to his home country of Mexico this month. Donovan plans to meet him there and start a new life.

“I am so overwhelmed by how gross the conditions are and how horrifyingly unregulated everything is,” Donovan said. “They can literally do whatever they want and nobody is checking, and it seems like nobody cares.”

All three of the deaths in the facility — in 2012, 2017 and 2022 — came after apparent lapses in medical care. One man died from opioid withdrawal after the facility cut off his prescribed medication. Another died of a heart attack after medical staff didn’t call an ambulance for an hour and a nurse was unfamiliar with the equipment needed to treat him, according to the ACLU. The third died of a blood clot after repeatedly complaining of pain in his leg.

Batooie has clogged arteries and takes blood thinners. An Iranian who came to the U.S. more than 20 years ago, he was arrested in June 2025 as he left his home in the Denver area for soccer practice. It was the same day that the U.S. began bombing Iran. Hundreds of Iranians were arrested nationwide, and as he waited to be processed, Batooie sat with eight or nine other Iranian immigrants.

He went without his medication periodically. At one point, he woke up with chest pain and called for help. None came, and other detainees began to bang on the doors, he said.

A guard peered through the cell window and left, Batooie said. He lay on the floor in pain until another guard came and he was later taken to the medical unit.

After his chest pain incident, the guard who ignored him was counseled, a supervisor wrote to Batooie in a grievance reviewed by The Post.

Aurora’s emergency medical services were called to the facility’s main address 168 times during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration, nearly 50 more calls than during the final 18 months of the Biden administration, call records show.

911 calls describe seizures, mental health crises and head injuries. A nurse told one dispatcher that a man who was hearing voices jumped from a toilet and hit his head.

Between October 2025 and the end of August, there were 188 hospital admissions, clinic appointments and emergency visits to UCHealth University of Colorado Hospital from the facility, said hospital spokesman Dan Weaver.

‘It damages us’

Attorneys and advocates argued that conditions in the facility were not accidental. Geo is one of the nation’s largest and most profitable private prison companies, and problems within its Aurora facility are well known.

“We’re detaining people at an extraordinary cost in large part because we are using detention as a way of brutalizing people in order to get them to self-deport,” said Chapin, the attorney and CU law professor. “The system wants people to give up and leave, and it’s been fairly effective, except we still have thousands and thousands of people in detention.”

Donovan’s husband Juan is one of nearly 4,000 Aurora detainees who’ve agreed to voluntarily depart the facility since Trump’s return to office, according to the Syracuse-based clearinghouse. There were 520 voluntary departures in July alone, the most in a single month in the 29 years of the clearinghouse’s data.

Aguirre, who came to the U.S. from El Salvador after he was bullied for studying to become a nurse, said one guard harangued detainees for fighting their cases.

“When he comes to our dorm, he’ll say things like, ‘Why are you fighting your case? You guys are animals, you guys need to leave this country,’ ” he said.

Unlike criminal cases, people in immigration court do not have the right to an attorney, meaning most are forced to navigate the complicated legal system alone.

Even if immigrants manage to secure representation, their attorneys’ ability to see clients inside the Aurora detention facility has grown considerably worse in the past few months, Sherman said.

On the south side of the facility where immigrant women are held, Sherman said, the facility either doesn’t have enough rooms or enough guards to monitor those rooms, meaning only one attorney can visit their client at a time.

“It might take someone four hours to meet with a client, even to have a 10-minute conversation, so if you think about all the work that person could be doing during that time, that just means we can’t help as many clients because we were spending so much time waiting and spinning our wheels,” Sherman said.

Noone, the immigration attorney, once worked in the Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Court. The holding facility used for alleged war criminals had yoga classes, pristine cells and an on-call medical service, drawing a contrast to the conditions at the civil detention center half a world away in Aurora.

She said she sees people with solid, winnable cases now considering voluntary departures as a means of survival.

“They’re just reading the temperature of the room and saying it doesn’t matter if their case is strong. If they’re there one more day, they may not make it,” Noone said. “Creating conditions under which survival is questionable, people are going to be more likely to self-deport. And that calculation is wild.”

In its unsigned statement, the Homeland Security Department said that “being in detention is a choice,” and it encouraged immigrants without legal status to self-deport.

Daniel does not want to return to Venezuela, where he believes he’ll be treated as a “traitor to the nation.” He was determined to fight his case and was grateful he still had the strength to do so.

But fighting is difficult. Before he was detained, in rare moments of downtime between working construction and cutting hair, he and his family went to the park, watched movies at a local theater in Aurora and visited the “beautiful scenery” of Red Rocks Amphitheatre. But when he goes to sleep now, he’s reminded that he’s not with his wife. He eats less. Talking to his family can be hard, their voices a reminder of the distance between them.

“It damages us,” he said of the effects of detention. “Not only psychologically, but our kids, our little ones.”

Aguirre said he’s cut off from this family and doesn’t know what’s happening to his son, his mother, his father and his brothers. He didn’t know how he would overcome what he’d experienced in detention.

“I don’t feel like I’m some type of criminal; I’m not a bad person. Even though I may have all these tattoos, I have a good heart,” he said. “And being locked up, wasting my time instead of helping my family or being with my son and teaching him a good example in life, it’s very hard for me.

“I wish I could speak to my kid,” Aguirre continued, “and say, ‘Hey son, I love you. One day we’ll be together, and this situation is going to end.’ ”

In a statement posted Saturday on X, DHS said ICE has initiated a “surge in sanctuary cities,” as part of the Trump administration’s continuous crackdown on immigration.

The states and jurisdictions identified by DHS include California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Washington, D.C., Illinois, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.

The statement comes a couple of days after federal officials shot a Venezuelan man in his car while he was delivering food for DoorDash in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garcas Perez was admitted to a hospital but has been under ICE’s custody with a bullet still lodged in his back.

Federal immigration agents have shot at least 20 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, seven of them fatally.

The shootings have sparked protests across the country.

Critics contend that Trump’s push to ramp up deportations has led to an increasing number of violent confrontations, and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved.

With the surge in ICE presence across the U.S., DHS officials said that they “will continue to arrest any and all illegal aliens that come into our path,” and claimed that they are targeting “criminal illegal aliens” who have been “released from jails by sanctuary politicians.”

Trump has committed to deporting “the worst of the worst,” but the vast majority of people arrested were non-criminal or had minor offenses.

Last week, a U.S. citizen was left bloodied and injured on the side of the road in a Chicago suburb after a confrontation with immigration enforcement agents who mistook him for a fugitive, according to local police and a resident who tried to help the man.

DHS called its recent plan to increase ICE presence in cities a “nationwide public safety surge.”

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this story.

AUSTIN (KXAN) — People gathered for another protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Sunday in north Austin, one week after a man was shot and injured by an ICE officer.

Austin immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who represents the man, identified him as Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28. Garcés Pérez, who is Venezuelan, had been working as a food delivery driver the day he was shot in north Austin.

The Party for Socialism & Liberation organized Sunday’s protest, writing on social media, “There is only one way we will get justice: if we rise up together and fight for it! We cannot wait: we must act now!”

text:
A federal judge denied a request for a preliminary injunction that would prevent the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting pretextual traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents.

U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger ruled the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition had not made a "clear showing" it was entitled to the injunction at this stage of the litigation. The ruling came Wednesday. Trauger was nominated to the bench by then-President Bill Clinton in 1998.

The coalition had sought the injunction as part of its ongoing challenge to the constitutionality of state troopers conducting traffic stops of motorists suspected of being noncitizens and then allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents -- riding along or stationed nearby -- to demand immigration papers and detain drivers.

The coalition, which filed suit in May against the Tennessee Highway Patrol and its oversight agency, the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security, is alleging the practice violates motorists' rights under the Fourth and 14th Amendments. Seven Tennessee residents joined as plaintiffs.

In a swift ruling, issued one day after a court hearing to consider arguments over the injunction, Trauger expressed deep skepticism that the immigrant coalition could ultimately demonstrate that the cooperative traffic stops violated motorists' rights under the Fourth Amendment, which protects individuals against unreasonable searches and seizures.

Trauger wrote the immigrant advocates had "no likelihood of success" on the claim "even if the court accepts as true that the THP troopers, pursuant to a policy, are pretextually pulling over non-White motorists in Memphis for the purpose of aiding ICE agents to investigate the motorists' immigration status."

"Supreme Court precedent is clear: a pretextual traffic stop supported by probable cause to believe a traffic violation has occurred does not violate the 4th Amendment, irrespective of the arresting officers' subjective intent," the judge continued.

Trauger gave more weight to the immigrant organization's allegation that the traffic stops violated drivers' 14th Amendment rights against discrimination, signalling the argument may have merit if supported by more evidence.

The evidence introduced thus far in the ongoing litigation "though not robust" is "sufficient to establish some likelihood of success on the merits" of the Fourteenth Amendment challenge to the traffic stop as "motivated by a discriminatory purpose" or having a "discriminatory effect," she wrote.

Trauger noted that data and evidence submitted to support allegations of discriminatory traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE focuses heavily on a weeklong operation in Nashville in May 2025 that resulted in scores of immigration arrests. That operation has formally ended, and Trauger indicated she needed more evidence of ongoing constitutional violations in the state, specifically in Memphis where the Highway Patrol is part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a multiagency effort including federal immigration enforcement, convened last fall by President Donald Trump.

Trauger also ruled the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition had a right to sue on behalf of its members, dismissing arguments by state lawyers that the organization lacked standing to pursue legal action.

title: DHS Says ICE Deportations Are Pushing Down Rent. Other Factors Are at Play - Newsweek
description:
“DHS is reducing your rent, especially in states that cooperate with [the Immigration and Custom Enforcement] ICE,” the department wrote in a social media post on X.
Read More on News DHS did not identify the source or methodology for the rent figures cited in its post.
In Austin, according to Zillow, the average rent is now $1,990, down $10 from a year earlier.
The U.S. construction industry employs nearly 1.6 million undocumented immigrants, according to reports based on U.S. Census data and labor surveys cited by the American Business Immigration Coalition.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has claimed that the Trump administration’s mass deportations of undocumented migrants has lowered rents in several Sun Belt cities, including Austin, Nashville and Phoenix.

“DHS is reducing your rent, especially in states that cooperate with [the Immigration and Custom Enforcement] ICE,” the department wrote in a social media post on X.

“Texas accounted for about a quarter of ICE arrests in July and posted the country’s sharpest rent drops, with San Antonio down 4.8 percent, Austin 4.3 percent, Dallas and Houston about 3 percent. Miami’s average rent is down 2.6 percent. Phoenix is down 4.2 percent. Atlanta is down 3.2 percent. Nashville is down 5.3 percent. New Orleans is down 8 percent,” it added.

Read More on News

DHS did not identify the source or methodology for the rent figures cited in its post. The percentages do not appear to correspond with several major publicly available rental indexes.

The post points at unspecified “research” showing that “illegal-worker inflows push rents and home prices up,” adding that “that inflow has been reversed in the states running the hardest interior enforcement.”

The research mentioned by the department is likely to be a working paper released by economists Daniel J. Wilson of the San Francisco Fed and Xiaoqing Zhou of the Dallas Fed earlier this year, which found that a surge in illegal immigration under President Joe Biden is what brought U.S. housing costs through the roof. The study’s conclusions were contested by other housing experts and economists, who pointed out at “inherent problems” with the authors’ methodology, including ignoring the impact of domestic migration on home price growth.

Nonetheless, the DHS concluded in its social media post: “Want lower cost of living: support mass deportations.”

While the administration wanted to highlight an alleged causal link between states willing to cooperate with ICE agents and lower rent, the metropolitan areas mentioned by the department were already undergoing a significant price correction due to a major new apartment and multifamily construction boom.

Newsweek contacted DHS for comment by email on Sunday.

A Supply Boom Outpaced Demand in the Sun Belt

Four of the metros where rent has fallen over the past year are in Texas, which has built more new apartment and multifamily housing than any other state since the pandemic in response to a surge in domestic migration between 2020 and 2022.

These included Austin, Dallas, Houston and San Antonio—all metros which were cited in an August 2025 study by RentCafe listing the top 20 cities for new apartment construction last year.

Dallas and Austin ranked second and third after New York City with 28,958 and 26,715 new units set to be completed by the end of the year, respectively. Phoenix, another city mentioned by DHS, was fourth with 21,188 units, while Atlanta followed in fifth place with 17,512. Miami was seventh with 15,666, Nashville was 14th with 9,810. New Orleans did not feature in the top 20.

All this inventory, approved during the surge in population and demand, flooded the market at a time when demand had already shrunk significantly under the pressure of higher prices and return-to-office orders from employers on the West and Northeast coasts.

The increased competition among landlords for a smaller pool of renters has led to a stark correction from peak pricing during the pandemic, and rent has been falling and continues sliding down in all of the metros cited above. In Austin, according to Zillow, the average rent is now $1,990, down $10 from a year earlier. In Dallas, it is $1,950, down $45 from a year earlier. In Houston, it is $1,900, unchanged from a year earlier. In San Antonio, it is $1,600, down $80 year-over-year.

In Miami, which remains a fairly expensive city for both renters and homebuyers, rent is $3,150, down $10 from a year earlier. In Phoenix, it is $1,825, down $70 year-over-year. In Atlanta, the average rent is $2,100, unchanged from a year earlier. In Nashville, it is $2,200, down $50 from a year earlier. In New Orleans, it is $1,650, down by a staggering $100 year-over-year, according to Zillow.

DHS did not provide metro-level figures showing how many renters had left Austin, Dallas, Houston or the other cities as a result of immigration enforcement, nor did it specify how much of each city’s rent decline can be attributed to deportations rather than other changes in housing supply and demand.

Crucially, the metros cited by DHS are also not the only ones now experiencing lower rent as a result of an oversupply of new housing units.

The same has been happening in Las Vegas, Nevada, and San Diego, California, a city in a purple state and another one in a blue state. In Las Vegas, the average rent is now $1,950, unchanged from last year, according to Zillow. In San Diego, it is $3,100, down $8 year-over-year.

Rent declines have not been confined to the Sun Belt, though there is where they have been most significant. Nationally, median asking rents for studios through two-bedroom properties across the 50 largest U.S. metro areas fell year-over-year for the 37th consecutive month in August, according to Realtor.com, driven by the combination of an influx of new apartments and slower rental demand, particularly in the South and West.

Can Mass Deportations Lower Rent?

Lowering the cost of housing through mass deportations of undocumented immigrants in the U.S. was one of President Donald Trump’s campaign promises in 2024. But experts have been skeptical about whether this could have the positive impact the president promised.

The Trump administration has deported more than 605,000 illegal aliens, while also triggering an additional 1.9 million self-deportations since January 2025, according to the White House.

From a housing-market perspective, large-scale deportations should “help free up some housing,” Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, said in an assessment of the policy earlier this year.

But any benefit gained from deporting masses of undocumented migrants could be undermined by the dire conditions it would leave the homebuilding workforce in. The U.S. construction industry employs nearly 1.6 million undocumented immigrants, according to reports based on U.S. Census data and labor surveys cited by the American Business Immigration Coalition. The Urban Institute reported last year that immigrants constituted more than 23 percent of U.S. construction workers in 2023 and estimated roughly half were undocumented.

“Immigrants play a significant role in construction, and reducing labor supply tends to raise building costs and slow new home production,” Fairweather said.

Restricting immigration carries the risk of making it “more difficult for companies to hire workers in the near-term, and that impact is likely to be acutely felt by a construction industry that employs many foreign-born workers,” Danielle Hale, Realtor.com chief economist, previously told Newsweek.

Similarly, the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) has argued that fewer available workers can delay construction, raise labor costs and ultimately put upward pressure on home prices. A July 2025 Reuters investigation found that a $20 million recreation center project near Mobile, Alabama, went from being on schedule to facing about a three-week delay after an ICE raid in Florida.

The superintendent said roughly half of his workforce stopped showing up, because workers feared similar raids. Reuters interviewed 14 people in construction and reported that they described delays, cost overruns and worsening labor shortages.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has denied media reports it has instructed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to stop arresting suspected illegal migrants who haven’t been accused of a crime, insisting “no one is off the table.”

The report was initially published by The Daily Wire, who citing “agency sources” said ICE officers had been told to only arrest illegal migrants with criminal convictions or charges.

President Trump has made a crackdown on illegal immigration one of the main policy pillars of his second term in office, though ICE has come in for significant criticism particularly following a series of deadly shootings involving its agents. A move to only target illegal migrants with criminal convictions or charges would be a major policy change, and would likely spark an angry reaction from a section of Trump’s political base.

Read More on News

On Saturday via X the DHS shared The Daily Wire’s report posted by its immigration reporter Jennie Taer adding: “This is false. No one is off the table. We will continue to arrest any and all illegal aliens that come into our path.

“Anyone in our country illegally will be arrested and deported.

“In an effort to protect American citizens, ICE has initiated a nationwide public safety surge in sanctuary cities where our brave officers will be targeting criminal illegal aliens—many released from jails by sanctuary politicians—including murderers, rapists, child predators, and gang members.”

Newsweek contacted the Department of Homeland Security for comment on Sunday via email outside of regular office hours.

The Daily Wire initially reported ICE agents across the United States were told over the weekend to end arrests of illegal migrants who don’t have criminal convictions or charges.

The publication said this would put an end to so-called “collateral arrests,” where officers pursuing a suspected criminal target could also detain other illegal migrants they came across.

Speaking to The Daily Wire one ICE officer said “they’re trying to calm things down before the [midterm] elections” while another commented: “I hope Trump finds out about this s*** and puts an end to it.”

Policy Confusion

Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin posted on X that he had spoken to nine ICE & DHS insiders who said “verbal guidance” was sent out to ICE offices instructing them to avoid non-criminal migrants, but this was “erroneous” resulting in a “miscommunication” about going after the “worst first.”

As a result, Melugin said there had been “no change in immigration enforcement policy” with guidance sent out to ICE field offices on Saturday night “to reaffirm this.”

Melugin also said he had spoken to President Trump who insisted anyone in the United States illegally remains “on the table” for ICE agents.

Immigration Polling

Public approval over Trump’s handling of immigration has fallen sharply in recent months with an Economist/YouGov poll tracker finding at the end of August it had fallen 24 points from plus 11 in February 2025 to minus 13.

The tracker found that in August just 40 percent of American adults approved of Trump’s handling of the issue, while 53 percent disapproved.

ICE Shootings

Over the past year ICE agents have been involved in a number of shootings, a number of them deadly, involving both suspected illegal migrants and anti-ICE protestors.

Earlier this month an ICE agent shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old DoorDash driver, but was not wearing his bodycam at the time.

Two anti-ICE activists, Renée Good and Alex Pretti, were shot dead by ICE officers during altercations in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in January.

In July the DHS told ICE agents to stop conducting traffic stops following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, though this was later overturned following criticism from Trump.

Since Trump returned to office in January 2025 illegal crossings of the U.S.-Mexican border have fallen dramatically to their lowest level since 1970.

text:
Misael Ramos, a democratic socialist running for City Council in Austin, was arrested by Texas troopers on Saturday morning for protesting US Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in the state's capital.

"At approximately 8:50 am this morning, two neighbors witnessed several state troopers, including many in unmarked vehicles, approach Misael while he was walking his dog and proceed to detain him," his campaign said on social media. "They never showed him a warrant for his arrest, but proceeded to arrest him anyway."

The Travis County Sheriff's Office website shows that the 40-year-old candidate for District 1 was booked at the county jail shortly after that and charged with a Class B misdemeanor for "riot participation." His campaign said the charge appears to be "related to his participation in the protest last Sunday at the site of Wilber's shooting by ICE."

The Austin American-Statesman reported that the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) could not be reached for comment.

"That these officers felt emboldened to do this to me, as a candidate on the ballot, speaks volumes to the level of impunity they feel to do this to our neighbors, who are living in fear of these kinds of abductions every day," Ramos said in a statement from jail. "We must end the terror in our communities created by the fascist administration in Washington and here in Texas—I will never stop standing up and speaking out for our community."

ABC affiliate KVUE reported that "at least four people were arrested by DPS and the Austin Police Department during Sunday's demonstration, including for charges of rioting, obstructing a highway, resisting arrest, and assault on a peace officer. Ramos' campaign said additional arrests have been made on DPS warrants throughout the week."

Ramos' campaign held a Saturday afternoon press conference outside the jail with representatives from various organizations, including the Austin chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)—which has endorsed him—as well as the Austin Lawyers Guild and Texas State Employees Union.

"People have a constitutional right to gather, speak, protest, and criticize the government," George Lobb, an attorney and spokesperson for the Austin Lawyers Guild, said in a statement ahead of that event. "Arresting someone does not establish that they committed a crime, and pretrial conditions must comply with the Constitution."

Ramos was released from jail during the press conference, eliciting cheers from the crowd gathered outside. He made his way to the podium, hugging audience members, and began by thanking everyone who "spoke up" and "spoke out" on Saturday, including a neighbor who recorded his arrest and notified people he asked her to contact.

"This should not be happening on our streets," but "this is why I fight," the candidate declared, reiterating that he was approached while walking his dog—which one officer threatened to shoot—and never shown a warrant. "Thank you again, and let's keep fighting."

The crowd broke out into chants of "this is what solidarity looks like," and "Fuck ICE, ICE OUT."

Protests have been held in Texas since an ICE agent shot Garcés Pérez during a traffic stop last Sunday while he was making DoorDash deliveries. A federal judge has temporarily barred the President Donald Trump's administration from deporting the 28-year-old Venezuelan, who remains in ICE custody, despite having a bullet lodged in his back, near his spine.

Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar (D-Texas), whose district includes Austin, visited Garcés Pérez at a detention center in Pearsall on Wednesday. Afterward, according to The New York Times, the congressman told reporters that a doctor has advised the immigrant to have surgery to remove the bullet.

"If Wilber and his wife decide that he needs to go through his surgery, then ICE needs to expedite his care," said Casar. "I am making it very clear to every part of the federal government that ICE needs to take the medical care of Wilber Garcés extremely seriously."
