text:
Congress faces a Sept. 30 deadline to reauthorize the Lautenberg Amendment, a refugee program that has, for decades, helped Jews escape antisemitism in Iran. But the Trump administration has effectively shut the program down, by closing the processing centers that allow it to work. An odd choice for an administration that rarely misses a chance to tell us how seriously it takes antisemitism.

The Lautenberg-Specter program was enacted in 1990 to help persecuted Jews and Christians in the Soviet Union reunite with family in the United States, then expanded in 2004 to include religious minorities in Iran. Congress has reauthorized it on a bipartisan basis ever since. The danger it was meant to answer has not gone away and, indeed, may have only become more inflamed. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) has called Iran “the worst source of antisemitism in the world.” The bipartisan U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom says Iran is sponsoring “a global campaign of antisemitism,” targeting Jews and Jewish sites. And yet the Trump administration has closed one of the few paths built specifically to help them, and others persecuted because of their faith, escape.

The Lautenberg-Specter program has hardly been an open door. For Iranian religious minorities, the way out began with someone already in the United States, a family member or friend willing to sponsor them and help support them once they arrived. Jews, Christians, Baha’is, Zoroastrians, and Sabean Mandaeans began their applications in Iran and, because the United States has no embassy there to interview them, those who reached the next stage left Iran for Austria.

There, the Resettlement Support Center in Vienna received their applications, prepared the documents, arranged interviews with U.S. government officials and mandatory medical examinations, and helped with the paperwork for their eventual placement in the United States, while American law enforcement carried out background and security checks.

More than 33,000 members of Iran’s religious minorities made it through that system between 2001 and 2025. When the State Department ended the grant that paid for the center, which the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society had run in partnership with the government for over 25 years, more than 14,000 Iranians were still in the pipeline. The society no longer knows what has happened to many of them. The organization lost access to the government data it used to follow individual cases when the processing center closed. Its public guidance now directs applicants seeking information about their cases to the State Department or their representatives in Congress.

The people waiting in the Lautenberg pipeline have had more reason to leave in the past year than ever before. Since the war with Israel began, Iranian authorities arrested more than 20,000 people, including members of the country’s Baha’i, Christian and Jewish minorities. Baha’is were arrested, interrogated and had their homes raided and property confiscated; even before the war, authorities in Urmia had sealed four Baha’i-owned businesses after their owners closed them to observe a religious holiday.

At least 35 Jews in Tehran and Shiraz were summoned and interrogated about relatives in Israel, and members of the Jewish community were arrested in three provinces, some facing accusations of espionage. At least 54 Christians were reportedly arrested in the month after the war. The campaign has reached beyond Iran as well. In January 2025, an officer in Iran’s Quds Force recruited a Georgian drug trafficker and offered him $200,000 to assassinate Rabbi Shneor Segal in Azerbaijan, a plot Azerbaijani authorities broke up before it could be carried out. Trump’s restrictions on travel from Iran even include an explicit exception for immigrant visas for “ethnic and religious minorities facing persecution in Iran.”

Trump has made antisemitism one of the causes of his second presidency. He has created a federal task force to combat it, ordered agencies to use the government’s legal powers against it, and promised to confront it “at home and abroad.” His administration has investigated universities, threatened billions of dollars in federal funding, and pursued foreign students over what it says is “violent anti-Semitic incidents on campus.”

Yet in Iran, where Jews have been interrogated about relatives in Israel, arrested on suspicion of espionage, and surveilled in their own synagogues, one of the oldest American programs for getting them out has been dismantled.

By the end of this month, Congress should reauthorize Lautenberg. The administration should refund and reopen the processing centers that support it. Fourteen thousand stranded people, and their families in America, are waiting to see whether Trump’s promises about fighting antisemitism abroad mean anything when Jews facing persecution actually need a way out.

Mia Emmunah Toubian is an Iranian American journalist and human-rights researcher whose work at Harvard Medical School investigated the treatment of women political prisoners in Iran. Jason Bryan Silverstein is a writer and anthropologist focused on health and human rights, and he directs the Media, Medicine, and Health Program at Harvard Medical School.

text:
A massive five- day ICE operation that netted 426 arrests across Indiana is fueling Hoosier Sen. Jim Banks’ push for Congress to cement President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown into law before a future administration can reverse course.

Banks hailed “Operation Safe Community: Indiana” in a Fox News Digital interview this week after federal immigration officers fanned out across his home state from Aug. 30 through Sept. 3, arresting 426 people with records involving sex crimes, assault, domestic violence, drug trafficking and weapons offenses, according to ICE.

“This is why Donald Trump was elected in 2024: for mass deportation,” Banks told Fox News Digital. “It was one of his key agenda items during the campaign. And in this case in Indiana, you see the direct result of it.”

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION’S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE’S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

ICE also credited cooperation with state and local law enforcement agencies in carrying out the operation, something Republicans have flagged as a key aspect to successful enforcement.

But Banks argued the operation also underscores a limitation of Trump’s crackdown: aggressive executive enforcement today does not guarantee that the same immigration policies survive the next administration.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO ‘WITHHOLD FUNDING’ FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

“It is important that we codify Trump border security measures and tough-on-immigration policies and make them the law of the land,” he said.

The busts build on the lawmaker’s seven-bill immigration package, previously reported by Fox News Digital, which targets issues including birthright citizenship, family-based immigration, H-1B visas, noncitizens’ CDLs and congressional authority over Temporary Protected Status (TPS) to limit judicial intervention.

“If this could happen in Indiana, it could happen anywhere,” he added, arguing that the opposition has made it tougher to achieve immigration goals after displacing ICE from the 2025 immigration appropriations legislation.

“They’ve made that one of their biggest priorities in this Congress to defund our federal law enforcement, to stop ICE from doing their job, to deport violent criminals who are here illegally,” he said.

OMAR’S NEW LEGISLATION TARGETING ICE SPARKS OUTRAGE WHEN THE INTERNET SEES WHAT’S IN IT: ‘UN-AMERICAN’

“So it is important that we codify Trump border security measures and tough-on-immigration policies and make them the law of the land so that the next time, God forbid, a Joe Biden ever gets elected back to the White House or someone that comes from that radical wing of the Democrat Party…”

Banks also directed his frustration at his own party, criticizing the Republican-led Senate for failing to advance separate election legislation that he says should be another priority.

Many on the right have pressed for passage of the SAVE Act, a bill requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

“That’s one of my biggest disappointments with this Republican Senate – we haven’t passed [it],” he said.

“I hope by the end of the year that we can find a way to pass it. I’m going to keep fighting for it, but at the end of the day, the Trump administration and the Department of Justice is doing a lot crack down on illegals voting in our elections.”

ICE Enforcement Division Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said the right to vote is the “cornerstone of democracy” in announcing the capture of Guatemalan national Helda Mendez-Merida for “poisoning our elections.”

text:
President Donald Trump sought on Friday to unilaterally withhold more than $800 million in spending on immigration, race and education that Congress has approved.

The move was the latest salvo in a fight between the Trump administration and Congress over control of the nation’s spending.

“President Trump is committed to utilizing all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens,” the White House said in a statement announcing the steps.

The statement outlined several programs, including some focused on refugee assistance, racial-minority business development and overseas conservation.

The Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, but the White House said the programs supported illegal immigration, stoked racial tensions and promoted alarmist approaches to the environment.

The White House is deploying a rarely used technique known as a “pocket rescission” that bypasses Congress.

Senator Susan Collins, who chairs the chamber’s Appropriations Committee, described the step as “illegal.”

“This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse,” said Collins, a member of Trump‘s Republican Party fighting a tight race for reelection in Maine. “Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law.”

The Supreme Court last year declined to block Trump from using the same tactic to withhold $4.9 billion in foreign aid Congress had approved, while litigation continued.

–

(Reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by William Mallard)

text:
Cattle industry groups are warning that immigration enforcement operations across Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas are disrupting the beef supply chain, delaying shipments of thousands of cattle, and generating millions of dollars in losses and additional costs, even as the Department of Homeland Security told Newsweek that ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas.

The Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a joint statement on September 24 that they were “closely monitoring” reported ICE activity affecting agricultural communities in the three states, warning that the enforcement activity was disrupting the livestock industry.

The groups said thousands of fed cattle that had been scheduled for shipment to processors were delayed, resulting in “millions of dollars in lost revenue and additional costs." They also reported workforce disruptions at feedyards, dairies, processors, feed and grain companies, transportation hubs and community services.

Read More on News

“These ICE operations are having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the cattle supply chain moving,” the associations said. They warned that the disruptions would lead to higher beef prices for consumers.

The average U.S. price of 100 percent ground beef was $6.92 per pound in August, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. President Donald Trump has faced growing pressure over his administration’s beef policies as consumers contend with high prices.

His approval rating has also fallen in several of the country’s biggest beef-producing states, including states he carried comfortably in the 2024 election. The administration has also turned its attention to major retailers as it seeks to address high beef prices. The Department of Justice is investigating beef pricing at eight major retailers, including Walmart.

The cattle groups said they recognize the federal government's responsibility to enforce immigration law but argued that sudden workforce disruptions can produce animal-welfare, operational, and economic consequences beyond the businesses directly affected.

DHS Points To Its Arrests

"ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas," a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek. "ICE law enforcement has conducted operations targeting heinous criminals including murderers, rapists, and drug traffickers and illegal aliens with final orders of removal."

DHS pointed to several recent ICE arrests in Kansas, including Flora Elvira De La Cruz Bustillos, a Mexican national arrested in Liberal who the agency said had convictions for cruelty toward a child and larceny.

The agency said Ky Sayapheth, a Laotian national arrested in Hutchinson, had been convicted of homicide, aggravated assault of a police officer with a weapon, aggravated assault with a weapon, and had escaped from custody.

DHS said Jose Garcia Villa, a Mexican national arrested in Dodge City, had convictions for kidnapping and sexual assault. The department also identified Kham Khamchanh, a Laotian national arrested in Hutchinson, who it said had been convicted of homicide.

The agency said Raul Duquenzne-Batista, a Cuban national arrested in Larned, had convictions including aggravated assault, kidnapping, burglary and rape.

Disruptions Adding To Other Problems

Cattle industry groups said the disruption comes amid existing pressures on the cattle and beef supply chain and argued that the effects can continue after individual enforcement operations have ended.

They called on federal officials to conduct immigration enforcement “in a lawful, orderly, and transparent manner,” respect due process and communicate clearly with employers and communities affected by enforcement activity.

Estimated U.S. cattle slaughter on September 24 was about 90,000 head, down from 107,000 a week earlier, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data reported by Reuters. Industry members told Reuters that immigration enforcement had kept meatpacking workers away from plants in Dodge City and Liberal, Kansas, contributing to delays in cattle shipments.

In Kansas, it dropped from plus 23 on January 20, 2025, to plus 2 on August 27, 2026, while Texas fell from plus 6 to minus 17 and Oklahoma from plus 31 to plus 7.

The analysis found little immediate change following Trump’s August 21 announcement allowing up to 300,000 metric tons of beef to enter the U.S. tariff-free for 90 days.

title: Who Killed Asylum? - Jacobin
description:
Each did so not by eliminating asylum outright but by slowly eroding the rights that asylum is supposed to grant.
Under the auspices of preventing “terrorists from abusing the asylum laws of the United States,” the act demanded that asylum seekers provide concrete documentation of persecution in their home countries.
As a result, gang violence, the main reason the vast majority of Central Americans sought refuge in the United States, no longer counted for asylum.
The logic was brutal in its simplicity: After 1980, in order to apply for asylum, migrants needed to be physically present in the United States.
Today only migrants from the last vestiges of communism stand a reasonable chance of receiving asylum in the United States.
text:
The modern concept of asylum was established in the aftermath of the Holocaust by what is known as the 1951 Refugee Convention. During the rise of the Third Reich, large numbers of Jewish émigrés fled Europe but were turned away by other countries, including the United States. Many later died in concentration camps. After World War II, asylum law was created to ensure that such a thing never happened again; anyone fleeing for their life would be guaranteed the right to seek protection in any other country on earth.

Except that’s never how it worked. Instead, the asylum system was driven by Cold War geopolitics to push an anti-communist, pro-capitalist agenda.

In fact, the USSR actually declined to sign the 1951 Refugee Convention, stating that it was simply another ideological tool “dictated by Western countries” to discredit socialist states. This was in essence correct. From 1951 to 1979, the US government overwhelmingly granted refugee status to people “from any Communist or Communist-dominated country or area.” This included some seven hundred thousand Cubans, four hundred thousand “Indochinese” (decamping after communist victories in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia), another four hundred thousand Eastern Bloc Europeans, eighty thousand Soviet dissidents, and almost no one else.

It wasn’t until the passage of the Refugee Act of 1980 that the US asylum system became what we are now accustomed to, with migrants applying individually on a case-by-case basis. Crucially, this new asylum was available to anyone unable to return to their country of origin or the country where they last resided due to “persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”

Still, throughout the 1980s, asylum approvals heavily favored applicants from communist countries while systematically rejecting those who were fleeing US-backed violence. Whereas refugees from Cuba and the USSR had 70 to 80 percent approval rates, Salvadorans and Guatemalans displaced by massacres and genocides funded by the Reagan administration had less than 3 percent.

It’s worth noting that, under Ronald Reagan, the United States resettled more refugees than all other countries in the world combined. Even Reagan’s border enforcement policies look alien compared to contemporary anti-immigrant legislation, with the vast majority of the border left loosely guarded in the 1980s. It was common knowledge at the time that the United States relied on undocumented Mexican seasonal labor to harvest its crops and did not need a hard border to discipline labor’s movement.

This likely informed Reagan’s decision to sign a bill that granted approximately 2.9 million migrants mass amnesty instead, the vast majority of them Central Americans and Mexicans. The decision had less to do with helping the victims of his disastrous Latin American policies than normalizing the labor market. While anyone who had entered the country before 1982 was allowed to remain in the country, farmworkers that had been employed for at least ninety days could also be legalized. Many of those amnestied were Salvadorans and Guatemalans who had already been denied asylum. As individuals, they were not worthy of asylum, but as an employable group, they were welcome to stay. The bill also put more money in border militarization initiatives and stricter employment guidelines.

Far from an act of kindness, this was again a calculated political one. Having burned much of Central America to the ground in the name of fighting communism, Reagan had no choice but to accept some of the people he had displaced.

At its core, then, the US asylum system has always been an ideological tool. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, and with it the gradual demise of the communist threat, the United States has been slowly dismantling it. Unlike the immigration system writ large, there is no serious material interest for capital in maintaining asylum.

Without the threat of socialism’s Second World, the capitalists of the First World no longer had to buy off supporters in the Third. And now that capitalism has no overt global competitor, and the United States has abandoned any effort to legitimize its role in the world, it no longer needs to respect the human rights it previously claimed to be protecting on behalf of the so-called free world.

The great unwinding of asylum did not happen immediately. In fact, asylum approval rates actually grew from 1991 to 2012. At the beginning of this period, the system was working at full capacity in order to put ideological pressure on a faltering USSR, whose migrants, fleeing the last gasps of the Soviet Bloc and the steep decline in living standards accompanying its transition to capitalism, were met with open arms.

Indeed, rising rates of asylum seekers accompanied the growing instability of a freshly capitalist-dominated world. After 1991, there was a steady increase in globally displaced persons due to “persecution, conflict, violence, human rights violations or events seriously disturbing public order.” By 2013, there were over fifty million displaced people worldwide, many of whom were forced to flee due to proxy wars started by the United States. In 2025, that number had climbed to nearly 120 million, reflecting a level of worldwide conflict not seen since World War II. And that doesn’t even account for the millions of people displaced by climate change, driven largely by Western extraction and consumption.

In response, there has been a bipartisan effort across five presidencies — those of Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden, and Donald Trump — to keep out the people displaced by failed neoliberal policy and US intervention abroad. Each did so not by eliminating asylum outright but by slowly eroding the rights that asylum is supposed to grant.

One of the first blows to asylum came in 1996, under Clinton, when Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA). Whereas migrants were previously guaranteed the right to ask for asylum at any time, they were now made to file for asylum within one year of arriving in the country. After that, their universal and enduring right to seek refuge from persecution would, paradoxically, expire. It was a wholly artificial barrier that served no purpose except to limit asylum protections. Clinton signed the law without hesitation.

A decade later, in 2005, Congress passed the REAL ID Act. Under the auspices of preventing “terrorists from abusing the asylum laws of the United States,” the act demanded that asylum seekers provide concrete documentation of persecution in their home countries. The problem, of course, is that people fleeing for their lives across thousands of miles are often unable to maintain such documents. Nor do murderers normally warn their victims in writing that they are about to kill them.

Though there was no evidence that terrorists had ever abused US asylum in the first place (none of the men involved in the 9/11 attacks were asylum seekers), the Bush-era policy set a precedent that asylum law was now a threat to national security. No longer needed to bludgeon communists, asylum was weakened to advance a new ideological war, and refugees became potential terrorists.

But asylum really began to weaken under Barack Obama. After asylum rates hit all-time highs in 2012, Republicans ramped up pressure on Obama’s reelection campaign by falsely claiming that he had created “open border” policies flooding America with undocumented migrants. Rather than stand his ground, Obama capitulated almost immediately, deporting over 407,000 people in 2012 alone and 3.1 million across eight years, more than any other president in history, including Trump.

Like Reagan before him, Obama specifically targeted Central Americans following failed US interventions in the region, most notably the Honduran coup supported by then–Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Under Obama, the court system was increasingly pressured to no longer recognize migrants fleeing gang violence as having a “credible fear” of losing their lives. As a result, gang violence, the main reason the vast majority of Central Americans sought refuge in the United States, no longer counted for asylum.

Perhaps Obama’s most insidious innovation, however, was the creation of the Southern Border Program (SBP) in 2014, which paid Mexico to catch and deport migrants before they could ever reach the United States. The logic was brutal in its simplicity: After 1980, in order to apply for asylum, migrants needed to be physically present in the United States. So if they were intercepted in Mexico first, they’d never have a chance to ask. In its first decade, SBP quietly denied millions of migrants the chance to apply, without impacting official asylum statistics.

Far from breaking from Obama, Trump continued down the path his predecessor paved. In 2018, Trump-nominated Attorney General Jeff Sessions ruled that gang violence no longer counted as “credible fear,” codifying what Obama had done out of sight. In 2019, the administration launched Remain in Mexico, which built on the logic of SBP by demanding that migrants had to first “apply to apply” for asylum, so to speak. Migrants would have to declare they wished to apply for asylum while still in Mexico, then wait there indefinitely until they were permitted to enter the United States and apply a second time. For most, waiting in a third country without access to work, social resources, or housing — especially in dangerous border cities — was an impossible demand. What Obama once did quietly, Trump did publicly and with relish.

Relatedly, in 2019 the Department of Justice also passed what is known as the “third country bar.” In short, the bar allows the United States to pass the asylum buck onto Mexico by requiring that migrants who travel through a third country (that is, not their home country, and not the United States, but an intermediary between the two) apply for asylum there first. Geography dictates that this almost always means Mexico. Now US immigration judges can immediately deny an asylum claim if they feel that a migrant did not do enough to seek asylum there, even though Mexico is still actively catching and deporting migrants under SBP. This policy continues to implicitly favor those few migrants still fleeing communism — Chinese and Cuban migrants are much more likely to travel directly to the United States by sea and so have no third country requirement.

Though liberals celebrated Biden for ending Remain in Mexico in 2022, less attention was paid to the fact that it was functionally replaced with a new phone application known as CBP One, which formalized and expanded the demand that migrants apply to apply for asylum. As soon as migrants entered Mexico, they were expected to download the CBP One application and take a geolocated photo of themselves daily in order to remain in the digital asylum line. Miss a day and they would be sent to the back of that line, which quickly grew to a wait of over six months. Migrants reported that the app frequently malfunctioned and crashed, losing their data and forcing them to start over after months of waiting in the third country.

When Trump was reelected in 2024, he immediately closed CBP One without creating a replacement, leaving tens of thousands of migrants stranded indefinitely in Mexico. This was especially heinous because, due to an agreement with the Mexican government, migrants who enrolled in CBP One were granted a one-year visa in Mexico. When CBP One was suddenly cut, everyone was made illegal overnight. There are no available records of how many people have been deported from Mexico as a result.

Weeks ago, the Supreme Court ruled to allow the United States to functionally eliminate all asylum protections for those fleeing US imperialism and intervention in Latin America. In Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, the court blessed the government’s use of a new “metering policy.” First invented and employed by the Obama and Biden administrations as another means of sidestepping asylum obligations, the policy permits an arbitrarily low number of migrants to enter the United States. Once that number is reached, the government can then refuse others to enter the country, and Trump can use images of those left behind to bolster his false claims of invasion.

The transformation of the refugee program from granting benefits (including labor market access) to denying them has created a pressure cooker at the border, with tens of thousands of people concentrated in Mexican border towns. A key aspect of refugee resettlement was that it strategically distributed refugees to stabilize rural and postindustrial depopulation. Its dismantling was a disaster that set the stage for localized anti-immigrant backlash. The image of the refugee was transformed from a neighbor building a new life next door to a faceless mass clamoring at the border, providing grist for Trumpian immigration panic.

Today only migrants from the last vestiges of communism stand a reasonable chance of receiving asylum in the United States. Venezuelans had a 72 percent approval rate in 2025, and Chinese applicants a 58 percent rate. Compare this to Indians’ 18 percent, despite Narendra Modi’s government, which is virulently anti-Muslim, being a key Trump ally.

text:
Immigrant rights advocates gathered outside of Republican Senator Ashley Moody's Orlando office Wednesday, urging her to support proposed legislation — already passed by the U.S. House — that would restore Temporary Protected Status for Haitians until 2029.

The Senate proposal seeks to restore Haiti's TPS, following its termination on July 27. House lawmakers — mostly Democrats, but also 10 Republicans, plus one Independent — voted 224-204 in April to approve companion legislation.

RELATED: Haitian TPS comes to an end, healthcare leaders fear the impact on long-term care

What's TPS?

TPS is a status designated for foreign countries where conditions temporarily prevent nationals from being able to return safely — or, in certain cases, for countries that can't adequately handle their returning nationals, according to the Department of Homeland Security. People hailing from a TPS-designated country who are already in the United States can become eligible to work here, and cannot be removed or detained based on their immigration status.

Haiti was designated for TPS in 2010, days after a massive earthquake devastated the country. It received multiple extensions of that status, in light of widespread violence and humanitarian crises which remain ongoing. The State Department urges U.S. citizens not to travel to Haiti for any reason, "due to crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care."

This year, Haiti's TPS was terminated July 27, under the direction of former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem. Since then, hundreds of Haitians have been deported from the U.S. to their home country, where they reportedly face dangerous conditions. Many deportees still had asylum claims pending with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to the international watchdog Human Rights Watch.

Concern in Central Florida

On Wednesday morning, Central Floridians with the Immigrants are Welcome Here Coalition and other advocacy groups held a rally outside Moody's Orlando office, to sound the alarm about challenges Haitians now face due to the termination of their TPS.

"People who lose legal status don't disappear; they get pushed into the shadows, where they are easier to exploit, easier to traffic, and less likely to report abuse," said Aaron Lewis, a community organizer with the coalition and the Justice and Power Collective.

"I work on homelessness, domestic violence, and trafficking every day. This policy feeds all three of them," Lewis said.

Advocates also flagged new whistleblower reports that allege detainees are experiencing inhumane conditions at an ICE holding facility in Orlando. This week, Democratic members of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform sent a letter with a comprehensive breakdown of those allegations to ICE Acting Director David Venturella.

The whistleblower reports allege ICE is "putting hundreds of people in very, very small cells, denying them access to (legal) counsel," according to John Barry, a staff attorney with the Orlando Center for Justice.

"Our tax money is going to fund this wave of repression and violence that is going to impact not just people of color, and not just immigrants. It's going to affect all of us," Barry said. "And not just in our pocketbook, but most importantly, our foundational, basic, constitutional rights."

The whistleblower reports accuse ICE of detaining people in Orlando "for days to weeks in abusive and life-threatening conditions." Holding facilities are primarily meant for "short-term confinement," meaning 12 hours or less, according to ICE.

RELATED: FHP asks for input on building detention centers throughout Florida

What's next?

Advocates on Wednesday delivered to Moody's office printed copies of some 2,000 petition signatures, which were collected online to urge action on Haitian TPS and other, related concerns about how immigration enforcement is being handled under President Donald Trump.

A representative for Moody's office reportedly told advocates they'd receive a response, without giving an anticipated timeline.

In response to a request for comment on advocates' concerns, a spokesperson for Moody's office directed Central Florida Public Media to comments Moody shared with WPLG Local10, a Miami TV station, back in July.

At that time, Moody reportedly said she'd been communicating with the Trump administration about alternatives for Haitians, telling WPLG: "We have got to start looking at these on a case-by-case basis."

Also back in late July, Moody's office sent an email to people who had signed the online petition urging for the restoration of Haiti's TPS. "As a nation founded by immigrants, I understand the important contributions immigrants have made, not only to our country, but especially to Florida's communities," that email reads in part.

In that email, Moody told petitioners she would keep their "thoughts in mind" as she considered relevant legislation.
